newsitem.title: HUNGARY: BOMB SUPPLIER SUSPECTS HELD IN HUNGARY GANG WAR.
newsitem.headline: BOMB SUPPLIER SUSPECTS HELD IN HUNGARY GANG WAR.

text.p: Hungarian police said on Friday they had detained two men who were likely to have sold hand grenades used in a spate of bombings in Budapest in the past two months.
Budapest police chief Janos Bodracska told a news conference on Friday that the detention on Thursday night of two men in possession of explosives may help the police explain the wave of attacks.
"This line appears to be suitable for throwing light on one or two bombing cases," he said.
Since September, Budapest citizens have been rattled by eleven bombings and five armed attacks against people who are believed to have become involved in a war of organised gangs.
One man was killed in the shootings and two more severely injured. The grenade attacks have not injured anyone but have caused serious damage.
The latest incident came on Friday morning when an unknown attacker first shot at a 52-year-old Budapest casino owner and then struck him with his gun before fleeing.
The two men held by the police in Thursday were caught in possession of packages containing 28 hand grenades and other explosive devices, Bodracska said.
The two men had admitted selling nine handgrenades and the police were now conducting house searches which have already unearthed a Stinger rocket in a house in a village in southwest Hungary.
The police chief added that the price of a handgrenade is currently some 10,000 forints ($60) in Budapest.
The gangland war began over a sum of 2.7 billion forints, borrowed by an underworld figure at high interest, Bodracska said.
"He used the money and the sum was dwindling, and when it got too low, he disappered," he said. "Now we cannot find him and (the gangs) can't either."

The police chief said investigations were advancing. He added that only gang members had been injured in the gang war, but admitted that the property of ordinary citizens, such as cars, have been damaged.
Bodracska denied press reports that the lack of progress in solving the crime spree had caused Interior Minister Gabor Kuncze to lose confidence in him.
He added, that Budapest was still a safe city compared with such European capitals as Bratislava or Berlin.
